Zagare Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Šiaulių apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. Zagare's Jewish community was one of the oldest in Lithuania and, until the end of the 19th century, was actually divided into two entirely separate communities — Old and New Zagare — each with its own rabbis, cantors, ritual slaughterers, and cemeteries. The town produced an extraordinary roster of internationally significant figures: Rabbi Israel Salanter, founder of the Musar movement in Orthodox Judaism, whose influence is documented at several other sites in this collection; Isaak Kikoin, a leading Soviet physicist; the Art Nouveau architect Paul Mandelstamm; Kalman Ze'ev Wissotzky, founder of Wissotzky Tea; the biochemist Phoebus Levene, a pioneer in the study of nucleic acids and DNA; and the linguist Chatzkel Lemchen. On October 2, 1941, the day after Yom Kippur, all the prisoners of Zagare's ghetto, together with Jews brought in from numerous other settlements documented throughout this collection, were taken to Naryshkin Park and shot — around 3,000 people in total. This is the older of Zagare's two Jewish cemeteries, first mentioned in records from 1748; 40 local Jews were shot directly at this cemetery in 1941.
